transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, um, thank you. So, I'm an event planner—well, I help plan meetings and conventions and stuff—and recently I've had to be a lot more front-and-center, which is normally fine. I mean, I really like my job. I just finished high school a couple of years ago and got right into this, but lately, it's just been... it's been really hard. We take all these photos at the events, you know, for social media and marketing and just general wrap-ups, and I am in a lot of them now. 

And I just... I came in because I cannot stop staring at this one specific part of my face in every single picture. It's just so uneven-looking. Like, incredibly uneven. I spend, I don't even know how long, just zooming in on my phone and staring at it, trying to figure out how to hide it or why it looks like that. I've pointed it out to my friends, my coworkers, literally anyone I feel comfortable enough to ask, and they all tell me they barely see anything, or that it looks completely normal. But I know what I'm seeing! It's just right there, and ever since I started having to be in front of people more at work, it's all I can focus on. It's completely ruining how I feel when I'm supposed to be running an event, and I just... I can't let it go, no matter what anyone says to me.
Is it just your appearance that's been bothering you, or are there other things that you've been worrying about or feeling are not right?

Um, no, not really. It’s... it’s honestly just this one thing about my face. I mean, my life is actually going really well otherwise, which I guess is why it’s so frustrating that I can’t just be happy and focus on it. Like I said, I got this job right out of high school, which was a huge deal because usually, you know, they want someone with a college degree or years of experience for event planning. But my boss, she really took a chance on me after I helped with this big charity gala when I was just interning, so work is honestly amazing. 

I love my friends, my family is super supportive, I don't have, like, crazy relationship drama or money problems or anything like that keeping me up at night. I'm not, you know, feeling down about my life in general or worrying about other stuff. It is literally just my appearance. If I could just fix this unevenness, or if it just didn't look so glaringly obvious, everything would be completely perfect. 

But instead, it just takes up all my mental energy. Like, even just yesterday, I was supposed to be finalizing a catering menu for a huge corporate retreat—like 300 people, lots of moving parts—and instead of focusing on the dietary restrictions spreadsheet like I needed to, I spent, I don't know, maybe forty-five minutes in the venue's bathroom mirror just staring at how the overhead lighting caught my face. I was trying to see if the fluorescent lights made the asymmetry look worse than it did in the photos we took last week. So, yeah, it's really just the way I look that's wrong. Everything else in my life is completely fine, I just can't enjoy it because of this.
Has your focus on this unevenness on your face affected your relationships with friends, family, or coworkers?

Um, well, with my friends and family, it's mostly just them getting a little exasperated because I keep asking them to look at my photos, but at work... yeah, it's definitely starting to cause some real friction with my coworkers and my boss. 

Like, just last week, for example, we were putting together the final promotional packets and event materials for this upcoming tech convention. It’s a really big deal for our agency. I was supposed to send the digital proofs over to the printer by 3 PM on Thursday. But the packet included these team photos from our last major event, and I just... I couldn't stop looking at my face in them. The asymmetry was just screaming at me. I sat there at my desk, and I kept zooming in, trying to see if I could crop it differently, or maybe adjust the contrast so the shadows didn't highlight the unevenness so much. I even tried swapping out the photo for an older one, but then the formatting of the whole page got completely messed up, and I had to try and fix that. Before I even realized what was happening, it was almost 5 PM, and I completely missed the planning deadline for the print run. My boss had to call the printing company and literally beg them to squeeze our order in, and she was so confused and frustrated with me because usually I'm so on top of my schedule.

And it's not just that one time, either. It's bleeding into my everyday tasks. Like, vendor calls used to be so quick—I'd just hop on a video call, finalize the floral arrangements or the AV setup, and be done in ten or fifteen minutes. But now, because I know they can see me on the camera, meeting prep takes me so much longer than it should. I spend at least twenty or thirty minutes before every single call just adjusting my webcam, moving my desk lamp around, trying to find an angle that hides how lopsided my face looks. And then during the call, I'm just staring at my little video square the entire time instead of looking at the vendor's presentation. Everything just takes me longer now. My coworkers are definitely starting to notice that I'm dragging my feet on things that used to take me no time at all, and I hate it. I really do. I worked so hard to get this job right out of high school, and I don't want them to think I'm slacking off, but I just get so paralyzed trying to manage how I look in these materials and on these calls.
Do you feel like your concerns about your face are affecting your ability to enjoy social interactions or relationships outside of work?

Um, outside of work? Well, I guess... I mean, I don't really think it's affecting my relationships, not exactly. Like, my friends are still my friends, you know? We still text all the time, we have our group chat where we send memes and TikToks and complain about things. And my family is still super close. We do Sunday dinners at my parents' house almost every week, and I still go to those. My mom makes this amazing roast, and my dad usually watches whatever game is on, and it's nice. It's really nice. I wouldn't say I'm, like, isolating myself from the people I care about. 

But, I mean, the enjoyment part... that's maybe a little trickier to answer. Because, like I said before, I do ask my friends about the photos a lot. Probably too much. Like, if we go out for brunch on a Saturday—which we try to do at least once a month, usually at this place downtown that has really good avocado toast and bottomless mimosas—we always take pictures. It's just what we do. And as soon as we take them, I have to look at them right away. I'll pull my friend Sarah aside, or my friend Jessica, and I'll be like, "Look at this one, look at how the light is hitting my face right here, doesn't it look so obvious?" And they'll sigh and tell me I look fine, but then I spend the rest of the brunch just thinking about it. I'll go to the bathroom like three times just to check the mirror, and I'm not really listening when Jessica is talking about her new boyfriend or when Sarah is complaining about her classes. 

So I'm still there, I'm still doing the social things, but I'm just so distracted by it. It's like this constant hum in the back of my mind. Even at Sunday dinner with my parents, if my mom tries to snap a candid picture of me and the dog, I panic a little bit. I make her show it to me immediately, and if I don't like it, I make her delete it right in front of me so I know it's gone. She gets annoyed, obviously, and tells me I'm being ridiculous, which just makes me feel worse. So, I don't know. I'm not hiding in my room or anything, I'm still seeing everyone, but I guess I'm not really enjoying it the way I used to because I'm just so hyper-focused on how I look in every single situation where a camera might come out or where someone might be looking at me too closely.
Do you think your concerns about your face are interfering with your ability to perform your job as an event planner?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, like I was kind of saying before with the whole webcam thing, it’s really starting to get in the way. It’s... well, it’s a lot of little things that just add up. Like, before I send out any event pictures for our client wrap-up reports, or even right before I join one of those vendor meetings, I just... I can't help it, I'll pull out my phone and open the front-facing camera. And I'll just sit at my desk checking my face over and over. 

I'll tilt my head a certain way, you know, just trying to find an angle where the unevenness doesn't look so completely obvious in the office lighting. And if we need to send reference photos of the venue setup that I happen to be in, I'll literally retake the photos a million times until I find one where my face doesn't look completely wrong. Or sometimes I get so stuck in my own head about it that I'll turn to Maya—she's the other junior coordinator who sits in the pod next to me—and I'll just flat out ask her if I look weird. I'll be like, "Maya, be honest, does this side of my jaw look super lopsided today?" And she's really sweet about it, but I know it puts her in an awkward position, and I know I ask her way too much. 

But I just get so trapped in this loop of checking my phone camera, tilting my head, asking Maya for reassurance... and it can just eat up so much time. Like, enough time that I'm actually starting to fall behind on my real planning stuff. The event timelines, the budget spreadsheets, following up with the linen rental places... those tasks just sit there on my desk while I'm obsessing over my phone screen. It's so frustrating because I know I have a million things to do, and event planning is all about time management, but it's like my brain won't let me move on to the actual work until I feel okay about how I look.
Do you think that others can see the unevenness in your face as clearly as you can?

Well, that's the thing, and honestly, that's kind of the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. Because if you ask them, they all say no. Everyone else says they barely see anything at all, or they'll give me these generic lines like, "Oh, nobody's face is perfectly symmetrical," which just feels like they're trying to placate me, you know? But to me, it is so glaringly obvious. 

It’s just gotten so much worse lately because I’ve had to be more in front of people at work. When I first started at the agency right out of high school, I was mostly just doing behind-the-scenes stuff—data entry, organizing the supply closet, confirming catering numbers over email, stuff like that where nobody really had to look at me. But now that I'm taking on more responsibility and I'm actually out there, like, managing the VIP registration tables or leading the venue walkthroughs with major clients, I just feel so incredibly exposed. 

And ever since that shift happened at work, I just... I cannot stop staring at this one uneven-looking part of my face in photos. I'll look at the event recaps or even just a quick group selfie the team took to post on the company Instagram, and while everyone else is looking at the overall picture or how nice the floral arrangements look in the background, my eyes just instantly lock onto that lopsided area. It’s like a magnet. I zoom in, and I just stare at it, and I can't comprehend how other people claim they don't see it when it's right there, practically ruining the whole picture. It just makes me feel like I'm completely losing my mind, because to me it's this huge, undeniable flaw, but they swear up and down they barely notice it.
Do you ever think that maybe your face looks fine and it's just your own perception that there's something wrong with it?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess I hear what you're saying, and I know that's exactly what my mom and Maya and everyone else is trying to tell me when they say they don't see it. But... how could it just be my perception? Like, when I wake up in the morning and go into my bathroom—I have this specific mirror in there, I actually installed these bright LED vanity lights around it last year when I moved into this apartment because I wanted good lighting for doing my makeup before work—when I stand there, it is just... it's right there. It's not a trick of the light or my imagination. I can literally see the exact way the left side of my jaw dips differently than the right, and it actually casts a physical shadow. You can't just imagine a shadow, you know? 

Sometimes, I mean, maybe for a split second, I'll try to force myself to think, "Okay, maybe everyone is right, maybe I'm just being crazy and it's fine." But then ten minutes later I'll be in the kitchen heating up my morning coffee, and I'll catch my reflection in the dark glass of the microwave door, or later I'll see myself in the window of the subway when we're going through a tunnel on my commute to the office, and my heart just completely drops all over again. Because it looks so undeniably real. It's not like some optical illusion I'm making up in my brain. It's my actual physical face. 

So, I mean, I really wish I could believe it was just my perception, because honestly that would be so much easier, wouldn't it? If I could just snap my fingers and suddenly see a normal, even face like everyone else supposedly sees. But I just don't see how it could be in my head when it's staring right back at me every single time I look.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you see in your face is not as noticeable to others as it is to you?

I mean... yeah, I guess like I was saying just a minute ago, that's exactly the disconnect. That's the whole frustrating part, and honestly, it's the main reason I even made this appointment to come see you in the first place. Because it's like... I know they *say* they don't notice it. My mom, Maya, everyone... they claim it's barely there or they don't see it at all. And maybe, just maybe, they really aren't scrutinizing it the exact same way I am, but... it's just so hard to wrap my head around. 

Because ever since I got shifted to doing more of the front-facing event stuff—like actually being out there at the registration tables, talking to the vendors and the VIPs in person instead of just hiding behind my computer doing spreadsheets in the back room—I just feel like it's on full display for the whole world. And then I see the photos. We take all these recap photos for the agency's portfolio or social media, and I literally cannot stop staring at that one uneven spot on my jaw. I'll zoom in on it on my phone, and it takes up my whole screen, and it is just so incredibly obvious to me. It ruins the whole picture. 

So when people tell me it's not noticeable to them... I just, I don't know if they're just being polite because they know I'm insecure about it, or if they're trying to spare my feelings, or if they really are somehow just blind to it. Because to me, it's the only thing I can see. I just keep thinking, how can they possibly *not* notice it when I can't stop staring at it? It just makes me feel so crazy, you know? Like we're looking at two completely different realities.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you see in your face isn't actually there?

I mean... no. Honestly, no. And I know I keep bringing this up, and I know I probably sound like a completely broken record today, but... that is exactly why I came in to see you in the first place. Because it *is* there. 

Like I was just saying about the whole shift at work—going from being safely behind a desk doing data entry to suddenly being the one out there handing out lanyards and greeting the VIPs—ever since that happened, I just cannot stop staring at this one uneven-looking part of my face in all the event photos. And I feel like, if it wasn't actually there, if it was just completely imaginary like some kind of hallucination, there wouldn't be anything for me to zoom in on, would there? 

But there is. I zoom in on my phone, and I stare at it, and it's a physical, undeniable thing right there on the screen. The pixels are literally different on one side of my jaw than the other. It's casting a shadow. So when everyone else—my mom, Maya, my coworkers—when they say they barely see anything at all, or when you ask if it's possible it's just not there... it just makes my chest so tight. Because I'm not making it up. I'm really, really not. 

I'll sit on my couch after a twelve-hour shift, and I'll pull up the gallery from the photographer we hired, and I will just stare and stare at that one lopsided spot for, I don't know, an hour sometimes. Just agonizing over it, zooming in and out, comparing the left side to the right side. If it wasn't real, how could I be seeing it so clearly? How could it be taking up so much of my time and energy? I just... I can't accept that it's not there. It has to be there, because I'm looking right at it. I could literally pull out my phone right now and show you the pictures from the gala last weekend, and you would see exactly what I mean. It's there.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of the unevenness is not based on how your face actually looks?

I just... I don't know how to answer that without sounding like I'm repeating myself for the hundredth time, but... no. I really don't think it's possible. Because how could my perception be completely divorced from reality? I mean, I'm not looking at a funhouse mirror, you know? I'm looking at regular mirrors, I'm looking at high-resolution digital photographs taken by professional photographers with DSLR cameras at these events. 

And like I was saying, I'll sit there on my couch—usually it's my gray sectional, I got it from IKEA, it's super comfortable but I just sink into it and get lost in my phone—and I'll pull up the gallery link the photographer sends us. And I look at the pictures of myself standing next to the floral arrangements or the registration desk, and it's right there. It's not like I'm projecting some internal feeling onto my face. I'm literally just observing what is physically present. 

I guess I just don't understand what you mean when you say my perception isn't based on how my face actually looks. Because my perception is literally *of* my face. When I zoom in on that one spot on my jaw, I'm looking at the actual pixels that make up the image of my face. I'm looking at the shadow that the uneven bone structure casts. It's not a feeling, it's a visual fact. So if my perception isn't based on how my face actually looks, then what is it based on? Because I'm not hallucinating. I know I'm not. I'm just looking really, really closely at something that everyone else is just glancing at. And when you look closely at something, you see the truth of it, right? You see the flaws that other people might miss when they're just walking past you in a busy convention hall. So, no, I just... I can't wrap my head around the idea that what I'm seeing isn't based on reality. It just doesn't make any sense to me.
Do you feel like your concerns about your face are impacting your overall quality of life?

I mean... yeah. Honestly, yes, it really is. It’s bleeding into everything, especially my job, which is supposed to be the thing I’m actually good at. Like, just last week, I actually missed part of a major planning deadline. Which is so incredibly unlike me, because usually I am totally obsessed with my spreadsheets and my timelines, and I pride myself on keeping everything running smoothly. 

But we got the proofs back for some of the new event materials—like the promotional flyers and the digital recap stuff we send out to the sponsors—and I happened to be in some of the shots from the registration table. And I just... I completely spiraled. I spent so much time dealing with how I looked in the event materials, just zooming in on my jaw, trying to figure out if I could get the graphic designer to crop me out or blur the background so it wouldn't look so obviously lopsided. The whole afternoon just vanished while I was agonizing over it, and I totally missed the cutoff to submit the finalized schedule to our director. 

And it’s not even just the big deadlines anymore, which is the really scary part. It’s the day-to-day stuff, too. Like, vendor calls and meeting prep take me so much longer than they should now. I used to just pick up the phone or walk into a meeting with the caterers or the AV team and just get straight to business. But now... if I have to prep for an in-person meeting, I'm spending twenty minutes in the office bathroom beforehand just trying to position my hair so it falls exactly right to hide that side of my face. Or if it's a video call with a vendor, I'm spending half an hour obsessing over the webcam angle and the ring light so the shadow doesn't highlight the unevenness. 

It just... it takes up so much of my time and my mental energy. I feel like I'm doing two full-time jobs—my actual event planning job, and then this whole other exhausting job of just trying to manage my face and hide it from everyone. So, yeah, I guess it really is impacting my life. It's just making everything so much harder than it used to be.
Do you think it's possible that a doctor or a plastic surgeon would not see the unevenness you're describing if they examined your face in person?

I mean... I guess I get why you’re asking that, especially since I already told you that everyone else says they barely see anything at all. But... no, I really don't think it's possible that a plastic surgeon wouldn't see it. A plastic surgeon is completely different from my mom or my coworkers. They’re literally trained to look at symmetry and bone structure, you know? They measure things. They map faces out. 

So, like I was saying earlier—and I know I keep coming back to this, but it’s the entire reason I came in to see you—ever since I’ve had to be more in front of people at work, doing the actual event hosting and greeting instead of just the background planning, I just... I cannot stop staring at this one uneven-looking part of my face in all those photos. It's all I see. And sure, regular people might be distracted by the convention chaos or the floral arrangements, or they're just trying to get their lanyard and get to their panel, but a doctor? Someone whose entire career is based on analyzing and fixing facial flaws? They would see it immediately. 

I've actually even thought about booking a consultation with one, just looking up reviews online late at night when I can't sleep, just so someone would finally validate what I'm looking at. Because if I sat in their chair, under those bright clinical lights, or if I showed them those exact same high-res photos I pull up on my couch every single night... they would see the shadow. They would see the unevenness right away. They wouldn't just brush it off and tell me I look fine like Maya does. They would look at my jaw and know exactly why I can't stop obsessing over it, because it is a physical reality that a trained professional would absolutely be able to spot.
Have you tried to hide or camouflage the unevenness on your face with makeup or other methods?

Makeup... I mean, I try, but you can't really contour away an actual structural issue, you know? I’ve watched, like, dozens of YouTube tutorials on jawline contouring, and I've bought all these expensive matte bronzers, but it just looks like a muddy smudge on my face because the physical unevenness is still there underneath it. So, mostly, my methods are more about... positioning, I guess? Like, managing my angles and just constantly, constantly monitoring it. 

It’s actually exhausting. Like, before I send out any event pictures to our marketing team, or even before I just join a standard video meeting with a vendor—like the linen suppliers or the AV guys—I have this whole routine that I can't seem to stop doing. I’ll pull out my phone and just keep checking my face in the front-facing camera. Over and over. I'll open the camera app, look at how the overhead office light is hitting my jaw, close it, try to focus on my spreadsheets, and then two minutes later I'm opening the camera app again because I need to make sure it doesn't look as bad as I think it does. 

And if I have to be in a photo for something, or if I'm trying to send a quick update shot from the venue floor, I will literally retake the photo fifty times. I have to tilt my head a very specific way—like, slightly down and angled to the left—so the shadow falls differently and kind of hides the lopsided part. If I don't tilt my head exactly right, it's ruined and it's all I can see. And then, even after all that posing and retaking, I'll still turn to a coworker and be like, "Does my face look weird in this? Is my jaw super obvious?" I ask them so much, and they always just sigh and say no, but I just have to check. I can't help it.

And honestly, doing all of this—the checking my phone camera, the retaking photos from a million angles, the tilting my head until my neck literally cramps, interrogating my coworkers about how I look—it just... it eats up so much time. Like I was saying earlier about missing that deadline, this is exactly why. I get so caught up in trying to camouflage it with my angles and checking my screen that an entire hour will just vanish, and I completely fall behind on my actual event planning stuff. I'll have urgent emails piling up from the caterers or the venue managers, and I'm just sitting there staring at my phone camera, trying to fix how my face looks.
Have you considered or actually consulted a dermatologist or plastic surgeon about the unevenness you see in your face?

I haven't actually gone to see one, no. I mean, I've thought about it. I've thought about it a lot, actually, like I mentioned before when I was talking about looking up reviews online late at night. I've spent hours—like, literally hours—scrolling through RealSelf and Yelp and all these different plastic surgery forums, just trying to find someone who specializes in jaw asymmetry or facial reconstruction, just looking at their before-and-after galleries to see if they've fixed someone who looks like me. 

But actually making the appointment? I just... I haven't been able to bring myself to do it. Part of it is the cost, honestly, because I know even just a consultation can be a few hundred dollars, and on an event planner's salary, especially since I'm only twenty and just starting out, that's a lot of money to drop just to have someone look at my face. And then, I guess... I guess part of me is terrified of what they would actually say. Like, what if I sit in that chair and the surgeon looks at me and says, "Wow, yes, your jaw is incredibly uneven, and it's going to take thousands of dollars and major surgery to fix it"? Because then it's real, you know? It's not just me obsessing in the bathroom mirror; it's a medical fact. 

And then the other part of me is terrified that they might say what everyone else says—that they don't see it, or that it's too minor to operate on. And if a plastic surgeon, someone who literally gets paid to fix faces, tells me they won't fix it... what do I do then? I'd just be stuck like this forever. So, no, I haven't actually talked to a dermatologist or a surgeon yet. I just keep researching them and looking at their websites and thinking about it, but I haven't actually picked up the phone to call one.
Do you think it's possible that a plastic surgeon would tell you that there's nothing significantly wrong with the shape of your face?

I mean... I don't know. I guess anything is technically possible, but... it's just really hard for me to even wrap my head around that. Like I was just saying, that is literally my absolute worst nightmare, sitting in that clinical chair and having them tell me it's fine. But do I actually think they would say there’s *nothing* significantly wrong? I just... I don't see how they could. 

Because when I look at those photos, especially the high-res ones from the convention floor where the lighting is just absolutely unforgiving, the shadow is right there. It’s not a trick of the light, it’s not just a bad angle, it is a physical reality of my bone structure. So if a surgeon—someone who went to medical school for years and years specifically to study faces and symmetry and aesthetics—if they looked at me, how could they possibly say there's nothing wrong? 

I feel like if they said that, they would either be lying to me to try and make me feel better, or... or maybe they would just mean it's not "significant" enough for *them* to want to operate on. Like, maybe to a surgeon, "significant" means a massive deformity, like a car accident victim or something, so my jaw doesn't seem like a big deal to them. But to me, it's completely derailing my life. It's making me miss deadlines with the caterers, it's making me avoid vendors, it's eating up hours of my day. So maybe they would use the word "significant" differently than I do? 

But honestly... no. I really just can't imagine a trained professional looking at my jaw and genuinely thinking it's perfectly fine and normal. I just can't see that happening. Because if they say nothing is wrong, then... then what does that mean? It would mean I'm just making it all up, and I know I'm not. I know exactly what I'm seeing every single time I open my front-facing camera. So, I don't know. Maybe it's possible they might turn me away because my case isn't extreme enough for a massive surgery, but I really don't think it's possible that they just wouldn't see the flaw at all.
Have you ever actually scheduled an appointment with a plastic surgeon or a dermatologist to discuss your concerns about your face?

No, like I... I think I just mentioned a second ago, I really haven't. I haven't actually made that call or booked anything. 

It's actually kind of ironic, because my entire job—literally my whole life as an event planner—is scheduling things. I book caterers, I schedule walk-throughs with venue managers, I lock down dates for AV setups months in advance, I manage spreadsheets full of timelines. I am so used to coordinating schedules and locking things in. But when it comes to this? I just completely freeze. 

I'll go on these surgeons' websites, right? And a lot of them have those online booking portals now, where you don't even have to talk to a receptionist on the phone, which you'd think would make it so much easier for me. And I will literally click on the "Request Consultation" button. I've gotten to the page where it shows the little calendar with the available dates, and I'll even click on, like, a Tuesday afternoon or whatever, and I'll start typing in my name, my phone number, my email address... 

And then my heart just starts pounding so hard, and I just stare at the screen. I start thinking about everything I just told you—the cost of it, the fear of what they'll actually say to my face, the absolute dread of sitting in a brightly lit waiting room where the receptionists are probably judging my jawline before I even get to the back room—and I just... I close the tab. I exit out of the browser completely. I'll just push my laptop away and try to go back to my event emails. 

So, no, to answer your question directly, I have never actually locked in an appointment. I get right up to the very edge of doing it, like, my finger is literally hovering over the mouse button to confirm the booking, but I always chicken out. I just can't bring myself to finalize it.
Have you ever experienced repetitive thoughts or behaviors outside of your concerns about your face that you felt compelled to do?

Um, no. I mean, not really? Not outside of... well, not outside of the whole jaw thing. 

I guess, I mean, obviously with my job, I have to be really detail-oriented. Like I was saying about the scheduling, I am constantly checking and double-checking things. I guess some people might look at how I organize my event timelines and think, "Wow, she's a little obsessed," because I color-code literally everything down to the minute for vendor arrivals. Like, if the AV team is supposed to load in at 8:00 AM, that cell on my spreadsheet is bright yellow, and if they aren't there by 8:05, I am already calling the foreman. And I do go over the seating charts and the dietary restrictions lists over and over again before a big banquet, just to make absolutely sure nobody gets served a peanut allergy meal or whatever. 

But that's... that's just being good at my job, you know? That's just being professional, especially because I'm only twenty and a lot of these older corporate clients already underestimate me, so I have to be perfect. It's not a compulsion. It's not like I feel this agonizing dread that the world is going to end if I don't check the spreadsheet one more time. Once the event starts and things are running, I can let it go. 

I definitely don't have any of those things where I have to, like, wash my hands a million times or check if the stove is turned off before I leave the apartment. My mom actually does that a little bit—she’ll check the front door lock like three or four times before we go anywhere—but I've never been like that at all. I don't have to count my steps or tap things or anything like that. 

It really is just my face. That is the one and only thing that I absolutely cannot turn off.
